channel.title: PsyDigest — psychiatry literature digest
channel.description: Summaries of new psychiatric research and guidelines

item.title: The Effect of Stimulant Medications on Symptom and Treatment Outcomes in Adults With Comorbid Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity and Substance Use Disorder: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The clinical question is whether stimulant medications are effective and safe for adults with co-occurring ADHD and substance use disorder (SUD), compared to non-stimulant or non-pharmacological treatments. This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesised randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and nonrandomised comparative studies (NRCS) to inform treatment guidelines for this high-risk population.
FINDINGS: Six RCTs and one NRCS (total N = 662) were included. No significant differences were found between stimulant and non-stimulant/non-pharmacological treatments for ADHD treatment adherence, substance use outcomes, SUD symptom change, or substance abstinence (low confidence). A pooled analysis of three studies showed no significant difference in Clinical Global Improvement (OR 1.27, 95% CI 0.32–5.09). Evidence was insufficient to draw conclusions on ADHD symptom change, SUD treatment adherence, medication misuse/diversion, depression, or anxiety. No difference in adverse events was observed, but strength of evidence was not assessed.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is small, heterogeneous, and of low to very low quality, limiting firm conclusions. The absence of clear harm signals from stimulants is reassuring but preliminary. The lack of robust data on efficacy and safety, particularly regarding misuse/diversion and long-term outcomes, means current practice should remain cautious and individualised. More high-quality RCTs with longer follow-up are urgently needed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: For now, stimulants can be cautiously considered for adults with co-occurring ADHD and SUD, especially long-acting formulations, but clinicians should monitor closely for misuse and diversion. Non-stimulants cannot be recommended based on current evidence. Shared decision-making and close follow-up are essential.

item.title: A comprehensive review of European clinical practice guidelines on psychological and cognitive assessment and support for cancer patients and their families.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review examined European clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) over the past 15 years to assess how they address psychological and cognitive assessment and support for cancer patients and their families, highlighting gaps in inclusivity and implementation.
FINDINGS: Thirty-eight CPGs were included, showing an increasing multidisciplinary focus primarily on adult cancer patients, with distress, anxiety, and depression as key targets. Common tools included the Distress Thermometer and Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale, while psychosocial support and counselling were the most recommended interventions. Digital and family-centred approaches were rarely mentioned, and heterogeneity was noted in evidence levels and recommendation strength.
INTERPRETATION: The review highlights a growing but inconsistent effort to integrate psycho-oncology into cancer care across Europe. Strengths include the breadth of included guidelines and focus on common symptoms, but weaknesses include limited inclusivity (e.g., underserved groups), scarce digital/family-centred interventions, and methodological heterogeneity. The evidence base for recommendations appears preliminary, with gaps in high-quality, standardised protocols.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should be aware that while psycho-oncological support is increasingly recommended, access may vary by region and guideline quality. Digital and family-centred interventions remain underutilised and warrant further development and evaluation.

item.title: A Scoping Review of Maternal Substance Use and Peer Support and Its Implications for Maternal Health Providers.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This scoping review examined the influence of recovery peer support specialists (RPSS) on maternal recovery, capacity, and opioid-related mortality among pregnant and postpartum women with opioid use disorder (OUD) in the United States, given the quadrupling of cases since 1999. It synthesized diverse study designs (e.g., cohorts, trials, qualitative studies) from 2000–2021 to assess the role of RPSS within a broader public health crisis.
FINDINGS: Across 14 included studies, early medication for OUD and mental health treatment, patient navigators, and RPSS were associated with positive maternal recovery outcomes. Parental support improved maternal capacity, while stigma and child separation had negative effects. Infant removal and untreated mental health were linked to opioid overdose mortality. RPSS were perceived as potentially beneficial for recovery, capacity, and mortality reduction, though research was sparse and lacked rigorous designs.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is preliminary and heterogeneous, relying on observational and qualitative studies with limited high-quality trials. The lack of controlled comparisons and potential confounding (e.g., co-occurring treatments) weakens causal inferences. While RPSS show promise, the paucity of robust data and reliance on perceived effectiveness preclude definitive conclusions. Anti-oppressive practices and early intervention are plausible supportive strategies, but require further research to confirm impact.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings suggest RPSS *may* aid maternal recovery and capacity, but clinical practice should not yet prioritize RPSS over evidence-based treatments (e.g., medications for OUD). Clinicians should remain cautious about overinterpreting preliminary data and advocate for integrated, stigma-free care while awaiting higher-quality evidence.

item.title: Effectiveness of rTMS vs. Pharmacotherapy in Late-Life Treatment-Resistant Depression: An Observational Study of Individual Participant Data From Two Randomized Clinical Trials.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study compared the effectiveness of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) versus pharmacotherapy (aripiprazole augmentation, bupropion augmentation, or switch to bupropion) in older adults (≥60 years) with late-life treatment-resistant depression (LL-TRD) using individual participant data from two randomized clinical trials. The clinical question was whether rTMS is a superior or more tolerable alternative to pharmacotherapy in this population.
FINDINGS: After adjusting for baseline differences, rTMS was associated with lower Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) scores at 10 weeks compared to aripiprazole augmentation (difference: 4.16 points, 95% CI=2.32–6.00), bupropion augmentation (difference: 6.08 points, 95% CI=4.06–8.09), and switch to bupropion (difference: 6.36 points, 95% CI=4.55–8.17). Response rates (≥50% MADRS reduction) were higher with rTMS: adjusted odds ratios (AOR) vs. aripiprazole augmentation (AOR=3.83, 95% CI=1.08–13.56), bupropion augmentation (AOR=4.87, 95% CI=1.15–20.68), and switch to bupropion (AOR=4.02, 95% CI=1.12–14.47). Headache was more common with rTMS.
INTERPRETATION: The study provides moderate-strength evidence that rTMS may outperform pharmacotherapy in LL-TRD at 10 weeks, with clinically meaningful differences in MADRS scores (~4–6 points) and higher response rates. However, the evidence is observational (pooled IPD from two RCTs with different designs), and residual confounding cannot be excluded despite propensity score weighting and regression adjustment. The short follow-up (10 weeks) limits conclusions on durability or long-term tolerability. The higher headache rate with rTMS is a tolerability concern.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings suggest rTMS could be considered earlier in treatment algorithms for LL-TRD, particularly where pharmacotherapy augmentation/switching is being contemplated. Clinicians should weigh the higher acute efficacy against the increased risk of headache and logistical demands of rTMS. Longer-term outcomes and comparative cost-effectiveness remain uncertain.

item.title: Change in HbA1c and weight after initiation of antipsychotic treatment in people with severe mental illness in England: an individual-level interrupted time-series analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This large retrospective interrupted time-series analysis (n=96 849) in England used electronic health records to quantify how HbA1c and weight change before and after the first oral second-generation antipsychotic prescription in adults aged 18–59 with severe mental illness (SMI).
FINDINGS: Pre-treatment, HbA1c rose by 0.01 mmol/mol per week (95 % CI 0.00–0.01) and weight by 0.02 kg per week (0.02–0.02). In the first 90 days after initiation, HbA1c increased by 0.12 mmol/mol per week (0.09–0.15) and weight by 0.21 kg per week (0.20–0.22). From day 91 to 2 years, HbA1c reverted to pre-treatment rates (0.01 mmol/mol per week, 0.00–0.01) while weight rose by 0.03 kg per week (0.02–0.03). Olanzapine showed the largest increases (HbA1c 0.18 mmol/mol/week, 0.12–0.25; weight 0.28 kg/week, 0.27–0.30). Among 918 with baseline prediabetes, 13.7 % developed type 2 diabetes within 2 years (cumulative incidence 19.0 %) versus 1.7 % (3.0 %) in those with normal baseline HbA1c.
INTERPRETATION: The study provides robust real-world evidence of a rapid, clinically relevant deterioration in glycaemic control and weight in the first 90 days after antipsychotic initiation, particularly with olanzapine and in women. Strengths include the large national dataset, prespecified stratification, and patient involvement. Limitations include missing data (only 24.9 % had HbA1c measurements), no causal confirmation, and potential residual confounding from unmeasured lifestyle factors. The observed 0.12 mmol/mol/week HbA1c rise and 0.21 kg/week weight gain are statistically significant and likely clinically meaningful, supporting early monitoring and risk-stratified follow-up.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Baseline and 12-week monitoring of both HbA1c and weight are justified, with closer surveillance for patients on olanzapine or those with prediabetes; intervention thresholds should be guided by absolute risk rather than isolated biomarker changes.

item.title: Nicotine: evolution, dependence, and the path to total quit: redefining cessation in a changing nicotine landscape.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines how the expanding range of nicotine products (ENDS, HTPs, pouches, medicinal nicotine) has changed patterns of dependence and cessation, questioning whether “smoking cessation” alone remains an adequate public-health endpoint.
FINDINGS: The review synthesises neurobiological, epidemiological and clinical evidence to argue that non-combustible products can reduce toxicant exposure when smokers switch completely, yet they may also sustain nicotine dependence, encourage dual use, and create new initiation pathways. It highlights that current cessation frameworks rarely target complete nicotine cessation (“Total Quit”) and calls for clearer distinctions between smoking cessation and nicotine cessation.
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative synthesis rather than a systematic review, this paper offers a conceptual reframing rather than quantitative effect sizes. Its strength lies in integrating diverse literatures to highlight an important policy and clinical gap, but the lack of systematic quality appraisal and absence of meta-analytic data limit the certainty of any specific claim. The proposed shift from smoking cessation to “Total Quit” is plausible but remains untested in controlled trials.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians may need to re-evaluate cessation goals for patients using non-combustible nicotine, considering whether to aim for complete nicotine abstinence (“Total Quit”) rather than simply stopping combustible cigarettes.

item.title: Reducing the risk of obesity, diabetes, and metabolic disorders in patients treated with antipsychotics - recommendations of the Polish Psychiatric Association Part II: diagnostics and pharmacological treatment.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The Polish Psychiatric Association (PTP) issued consensus recommendations on diagnosing and managing metabolic risks in patients receiving antipsychotics (APs), where certain drugs increase obesity, diabetes, and metabolic disorder risk. This guideline is the second part of recommendations, focusing on diagnostics and pharmacological treatment.
FINDINGS: The guideline recommends baseline cardiometabolic assessment (weight, waist circumference, blood pressure, fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipid profile) before AP initiation, at 6 and 12 weeks, and annually thereafter. For patients with weight gain, abnormal tests, multiple risk factors, or starting high-risk APs (e.g., olanzapine, clozapine), metformin 1,000–2,000 mg/day is suggested as a safe, cost-effective preventive strategy. Obesity should be managed per current guidelines.
INTERPRETATION: This is a narrative consensus guideline, not based on new empirical data. Strengths include clear, practical monitoring and intervention timelines and endorsement of metformin as a preventive measure with moderate evidence. Limitations include lack of systematic evidence synthesis, absence of effect sizes or p-values, and potential bias from expert consensus without external validation. The clinical recommendations are consistent with international guidance but remain based on low-grade evidence.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The guideline supports structured metabolic monitoring and early metformin use in high-risk patients on APs. Clinicians should integrate these recommendations into routine practice while remaining cautious about extrapolating beyond the evidence base.

item.title: Promoting psychological resilience during the perinatal period with a digital tool (the HealthyMoms4MentalHealth-app): a study protocol for a randomised controlled trial in Sweden.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The trial will test whether a newly developed digital app (HealthyMoms4MentalHealth) can increase psychological resilience in 440 pregnant Swedish women (12–14 gestational weeks) compared with an active control app. The study is a two-arm parallel-group RCT designed to fill a gap in evaluated, scalable perinatal digital interventions.
FINDINGS: The trial is ongoing; no outcome data are yet available. The protocol specifies primary outcome (resilience) and secondary outcomes (wellbeing, depressive symptoms) measured at late pregnancy (35–37 weeks) and postpartum (8–9 weeks). The intervention is grounded in positive psychology and self-compassion theory and runs from mid-pregnancy to 8 weeks postpartum.
INTERPRETATION: Because this is a study protocol, no results exist to interpret. The design appears robust (randomisation, active control, pre-specified outcomes), but effectiveness remains unknown until data are published. External validity will depend on recruitment source (likely antenatal clinics) and uptake among diverse perinatal populations.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: No change in practice is warranted yet. Once results are available, clinicians should assess whether any observed effect on resilience translates into clinically meaningful improvements in wellbeing or depressive symptoms before integrating the app into routine perinatal care.

item.title: Cortisol and cognition in psychotic disorders: A systematic review and multi-level meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and multi-level meta-analysis investigated whether dysregulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, particularly cortisol, is associated with cognitive deficits in psychotic disorders. Twelve studies (940 participants) were included, with nine studies (822 participants) contributing to meta-analyses examining associations between basal cortisol levels and various cognitive domains.
FINDINGS: The meta-analyses found a significant negative association between afternoon/evening cortisol levels and executive functioning (EF) (r = -0.27, 95% CI [-0.42, -0.12], p = .01). Cortisol sampling time significantly moderated this relationship (F = 10.98, p = .004). No other robust associations between basal cortisol and cognition were observed. Sensitivity analyses suggested a negative association between morning cortisol and attention/working memory/processing speed (AWP) after excluding an influential study.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests that the relationship between cortisol and cognition in psychotic disorders is domain- and sampling-time-specific, rather than a general association. The strength of the evidence is moderate, with a small effect size (r = -0.27) that may not translate to clinically meaningful differences. The study highlights the need for more precise assessments of cortisol dynamics to clarify its role in cognitive impairment. Limitations include heterogeneity in cortisol sampling methods and cognitive assessments, as well as potential confounding factors not fully addressed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support routine measurement of basal cortisol to assess cognitive deficits in psychotic disorders. Clinicians should be cautious about inferring cognitive impairment based on cortisol levels alone. Further research is needed to determine if interventions targeting HPA-axis dysregulation could improve cognition in these patients.

item.title: Caring Letters and Suicide Mortality Among US Veterans Who Contacted the Veterans Crisis Line: A Prespecified Secondary Analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examined whether Caring Letters (CL) sent to US veterans who contacted the Veterans Crisis Line (VCL) reduced suicide mortality, building on earlier RCT evidence but using a larger, real-world cohort. It compared veterans who received CL (randomized to clinician or peer signatory) with a historical control group who did not receive CL.
FINDINGS: The analysis included 227,502 veterans (mean age 53.6 years; 84.4% men). Suicide mortality was 0.29% in the CL group (n=87,926) and 0.27% in the historical control group (n=139,576), with no significant difference (P = .31). Within the CL group, suicide rates were similar for peer-letter (0.21%) and clinician-letter recipients (0.22%; P = .95).
INTERPRETATION: This large, pragmatic study found no association between CL and suicide mortality, contrasting with earlier RCT findings. The lack of effect may reflect differences in population (real-world vs. RCT), intervention delivery, or statistical power (only 625 suicides observed). The historical control design introduces potential confounding, and subgroup analyses were not powered for mortality. The parent trial reported increased healthcare utilization, suggesting possible indirect benefits not captured here.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: CL should not be assumed to reduce suicide mortality in this population based on these findings. Clinicians should continue standard suicide prevention practices while awaiting further research on alternative interventions or mechanisms (e.g., healthcare engagement).

item.title: Woebot for Postpartum Mood and Anxiety: Randomized Controlled Trial Evaluating Feasibility, Acceptability, and Preliminary Efficacy of a Mobile Cognitive Behavioral Therapy Intervention.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This randomized controlled trial (RCT) tested the feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary efficacy of Woebot for Postpartum Mood and Anxiety (W-PPMA), a smartphone-based cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT)-informed digital intervention, in postpartum individuals (<3 months post partum) with elevated depressive symptoms. The study aimed to address treatment gaps in postpartum mental health, particularly among marginalized groups.
FINDINGS: Of 267 participants (W-PPMA: n=144; waitlist: n=123), median app engagement was 9 days (IQR 5–24) over 4 active weeks. At 8 weeks, W-PPMA users reported high feasibility (median 31, IQR 28–34), acceptability (median 30, IQR 28–34), and satisfaction (median 26, IQR 24–29). Among those with baseline depressive symptoms (n=97), PHQ-8 scores improved modestly in W-PPMA vs waitlist (mean change -0.7 vs 0.0; Cohen d = -0.16). Exploratory analyses showed a statistically significant reduction in perceived stress (mean difference -1.59, 95% CI -2.4 to -0.73) but no significant difference in EPDS change (mean difference -0.51, 95% CI -1.36 to 0.34).
INTERPRETATION: The study demonstrates high feasibility and acceptability of W-PPMA, with strong engagement metrics and user satisfaction. However, the preliminary efficacy on depressive symptoms was small (Cohen d = -0.16) and not statistically significant for EPDS. The observed reduction in perceived stress is modest and exploratory, requiring confirmation in larger, adequately powered trials. The sample was predominantly White (68.5%), limiting generalizability to more diverse populations. Funding sources and blinding status were not reported, introducing potential bias risks.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: W-PPMA shows promise as an accessible, acceptable digital intervention for postpartum mood and anxiety, particularly for stress reduction. However, current evidence does not support its efficacy for reducing depressive symptoms. Further research is needed before recommending W-PPMA as a routine clinical tool.

item.title: GLP-1 receptor agonist initiation and risk of psychiatric hospitalisation and emergency department presentation in adults with schizophrenia and type 2 diabetes in the USA: an observational cohort study using electronic health records data.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This observational cohort study (n=70 257) examined whether initiating GLP-1 receptor agonists in adults with schizophrenia and type 2 diabetes was associated with reduced psychiatric hospitalisation or emergency department (ED) presentations compared with initiating DPP-4 inhibitors, SGLT2 inhibitors, or no initiation.
FINDINGS: GLP-1 initiation was linked to lower risk of psychiatric hospitalisation versus non-initiation (HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.71–0.82), DPP-4 inhibitors (HR 0.82, 95% CI 0.75–0.90), and SGLT2 inhibitors (HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.78–0.88). It was also associated with fewer ED presentations versus non-initiation (HR 0.71, 95% CI 0.65–0.77), DPP-4 inhibitors (HR 0.87, 95% CI 0.80–0.95), and SGLT2 inhibitors (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.73–0.88).
INTERPRETATION: The associations suggest potential psychiatric benefits of GLP-1 agonists beyond metabolic effects, but residual confounding and selection bias limit causal inference. The effect sizes (HRs ~0.7–0.8) are statistically significant but modest; clinical significance depends on baseline risk and resource implications. Randomised trials are needed to confirm whether these agents reduce acute psychiatric care use or improve outcomes.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: GLP-1 agonists may offer a secondary benefit in reducing psychiatric crises for patients with schizophrenia and type 2 diabetes, but should not replace established psychiatric treatments. Monitor for gastrointestinal side effects and ensure metabolic monitoring is integrated into psychiatric care.

item.title: Pharmacological and Nonpharmacological Interventions to Address Insomnia Symptoms and Poor Sleep Quality Among People With HIV: Protocol for a Scoping Review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Insomnia and poor sleep quality are common among adults living with HIV and may worsen immune function, mental health, and adherence to antiretroviral therapy. This is a protocol for a scoping review aiming to map pharmacological and nonpharmacological interventions tested specifically in people with HIV aged ≥18 years.
FINDINGS: The review will include any study design (RCTs, observational, case series, protocols) that evaluates an intervention targeting sleep quality or insomnia symptoms in adults with HIV. Two independent reviewers will screen titles, abstracts, and full texts using Covidence, with consensus meetings to resolve disagreements. Data extraction will cover participant characteristics, intervention details, and sleep outcomes, with results synthesized narratively and tabulated. The team anticipates completing full-text reviews by January 2027 and publishing findings in mid-2027.
INTERPRETATION: As a scoping review protocol, this study does not present results and cannot assess effect sizes or efficacy. Its strength lies in the broad, systematic approach to mapping the evidence base, but conclusions will be limited by the heterogeneity of included studies and lack of quality appraisal. The findings will clarify which interventions have been studied in this population and identify gaps, but will not determine clinical effectiveness.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This review may guide clinicians toward interventions with preliminary evidence in people with HIV, but until efficacy data are synthesized and appraised, treatment decisions should rely on general insomnia guidelines and individual patient factors.

item.title: Online Sports Betting Legalization and Behavioral Health Care Use.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examined whether legalizing online sports betting in US states (2018–2022) was associated with increased use of mental health and substance use disorder (SUD) treatments, using a quasi-experimental difference-in-differences design in a large national claims dataset (2016–2023) of adults aged 18–64 with employer-sponsored insurance.
FINDINGS: Among 61,951,305 enrollee-years, legalization was linked to small but statistically significant increases in antidepressant use (men: +0.57 percentage points [95% CI, 0.26–0.89]; women: +1.08 [95% CI, 0.23–1.94]) and antianxiety medication use (men: +0.32 [95% CI, 0.14–0.50]; women: +0.64 [95% CI, 0.16–1.12]). Outpatient depression/anxiety diagnoses also rose (e.g., depression in women: +0.57 [95% CI, 0.25–0.89]). No significant changes were observed for SUD-related outcomes or emergency/inpatient diagnoses.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests a modest association between legalization and increased outpatient mental health service use, but causality cannot be inferred due to the observational design. The small effect sizes (sub-1 percentage point increases) raise questions about clinical significance, though they may reflect broader trends in mental health care access. Limitations include reliance on claims data (no clinical validation), lack of adjustment for unmeasured confounders (e.g., state-level mental health policies), and generalizability only to insured adults.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The findings do not mandate immediate changes in practice but highlight the need to monitor gambling-related harms in outpatient settings and consider preventive strategies in states legalizing online sports betting. Further research should assess long-term impacts and populations beyond the insured.

item.title: Protocol for a cluster randomized controlled trial among young people and their peers to reduce substance use and inequitable gender beliefs in Southern Africa.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study is a cluster randomized controlled trial (cRCT) designed to test whether an 8-session peer-group intervention (PEGISUS), embedded within vocational training (VT) programs in Zambia, Zimbabwe, and South Africa, can reduce substance use and promote equitable gender beliefs among young people aged 16–24 years who use substances together weekly or binge drink at least monthly. The trial aims to address social and structural factors (e.g., peer influence, socioeconomic adversity) that existing interventions often overlook, with assessments at baseline, 12 weeks, and 24 weeks.
FINDINGS: The primary outcome is the between-group mean difference in change in the total substance use involvement score on the ASSIST from baseline to 12 weeks. Secondary outcomes include changes in other substance use measures, gender-equitable beliefs (GEMS), and vocational training attendance, employment status, and income at 24 weeks. The trial will randomize 66 peer groups (~264 participants) in a 1:1 ratio to PEGISUS plus standard VT or standard VT alone (with referral for substance use services). The study is registered (NCT06489899, PACTR202502629432188) and powered for superiority.
INTERPRETATION: This is a well-designed cRCT with a clear rationale, appropriate randomization at the cluster level, and relevant outcomes addressing both substance use and gender norms. Strengths include embedding the intervention within existing VT programs, which may enhance sustainability and scalability. However, the trial is still ongoing (no results reported), so internal validity (e.g., blinding, attrition) and external validity (generalizability beyond VT programs) remain untested. The clinical significance will depend on the magnitude of effect sizes (e.g., ASSIST score reductions) and whether changes in gender-equitable beliefs translate into measurable behavioral outcomes.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: If effective, PEGISUS could offer a scalable, peer-based approach to reduce substance use and promote gender equity among at-risk youth in Southern Africa, particularly within vocational training settings. Clinicians should await peer-reviewed results before considering adoption, as current evidence is preliminary.

item.title: The critical role of maxillofacial surgeons in pain prevention and opioid consumption reduction.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines whether non-opioid, multimodal pain-management strategies in oral and maxillofacial surgery (OMS) can reduce postoperative opioid consumption while maintaining adequate analgesia. The review synthesizes studies published 2019-2024 across procedures such as orthognathic surgery, trauma, and dento-alveolar surgery.
FINDINGS: From 4 306 screened records, 102 studies were included. Thematic synthesis indicates that multimodal analgesia (e.g., NSAIDs, acetaminophen, gabapentinoids, regional nerve blocks) and pre-emptive regimens reduce opioid requirements without compromising pain control. Reported benefits include lower rates of postoperative nausea and vomiting, but quantitative effect sizes and confidence intervals are not provided in the abstract.
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative review without meta-analysis, the strength of evidence is limited by selection bias, lack of quantitative pooling, and absence of formal risk-of-bias assessment. The conclusion that non-opioid strategies “significantly reduce opioid dependence” is plausible but not quantified here. The review’s focus on recent literature and broad inclusion of OMS procedures improves face validity, yet generalizability to psychiatric patients is uncertain because the population is entirely surgical.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: For maxillofacial surgeons, the synthesis supports adopting multimodal, opioid-sparing protocols; however, psychiatrists should note this evidence does not directly address psychiatric populations or psychiatric prescribing practices.

item.title: Long-term health, criminal justice, and socioeconomic outcomes among people subject to compulsory mental health care in Norway: a nationwide registry cohort study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This nationwide registry cohort study in Norway examined long-term outcomes (health, criminal justice, socioeconomic) among adults subjected to different forms of compulsory mental health care (community treatment orders [CTOs], compulsory hospitalisation, compulsory observation) compared with those receiving voluntary care and the general population.
FINDINGS: The cohort included 321 708 individuals (mean age 36.5 years; 60.1% female). Compulsory care groups showed substantially worse outcomes across all domains than voluntary care and the general population. For example, self-harm/suicide was recorded in 12.1% of women and 5.7% of men in compulsory observation (adjusted probabilities 12% [95% CI 10–14] and 5.5% [4.4–6.9], respectively). Substance use disorder was present in 39.1% of women and 53.2% of men in compulsory observation (39% [36–42] and 53% [50–56]). Charges/imprisonment for violent or sexual offences were more common in men (37.4% [34–40]) than women (14.2% [12–16]). The CTO group had the highest adjusted probability of receiving disability benefits (89–93%). Suicide and external causes accounted for 55.7% of deaths in compulsory observation, compared with 38.2% in voluntary care and 18.6% in the general population.
INTERPRETATION: The study provides robust population-level evidence that compulsory care groups have poorer long-term outcomes than voluntary care and the general population. Strengths include nationwide coverage, long follow-up, and adjustment for birth year. However, residual confounding (e.g., severity of illness, socioeconomic factors) and lack of ethnicity data limit causal inference. The findings underscore that compulsory care groups are heterogeneous and should not be treated as a single prognostic entity. The clinical significance is high for service planning, but causality and modifiable risk factors remain uncertain.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These results highlight the need for targeted, long-term support for individuals subjected to compulsory care, particularly those under compulsory observation. Clinicians should prioritise integrated care addressing self-harm risk, substance use, and socioeconomic stability. However, the study does not establish whether compulsory care itself drives poor outcomes or merely identifies high-risk individuals.

item.title: Examinations of the heterogeneity in the structural brain connectome in schizophrenia.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This cross-sectional neuroimaging study examined whether structural brain dysconnectivity in schizophrenia (SCZ) reflects biologically and clinically meaningful subtypes. It compared 105 SCZ patients with 97 healthy controls using MRI and clinical assessments, then applied data-driven subtyping to the patient group.
FINDINGS: The authors report a subnetwork with increased inter-individual variability in SCZ, involving ventral-attention, frontal-parietal, and default-mode networks. Two SCZ subtypes emerged; subtype-II showed nominally more severe positive symptoms (t = 2.272, P = 0.025), lower neutrophil/lymphocyte ratio (t = –2.383, P = 0.025), better olanzapine response (t = 2.366, P = 0.021), and greater short-term improvement (t = 3.509, P = 0.006). Subtype-II also had distinct cortical thickness patterns and epicenters (e.g., left posterior cingulate).
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is preliminary. The study is observational, unadjusted for multiple comparisons (nominal P-values), and lacks replication or prospective validation. Effect sizes are not reported, and the clinical measures are post-hoc. The neuroimaging signal is biologically plausible but does not yet translate into actionable patient-level decisions.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: At present, these findings do not change routine care. They suggest a potential future role for connectome-based subtyping, but validation in larger, longitudinal cohorts with correction for multiple testing is required before any bedside application.

item.title: Short-Term Prognosis in Adolescents and Adults with Major Depressive Disorder and Associated Psychosocial Factors: A Prospective Study.
item.description: This prospective study examined whether short-term treatment outcomes differ between adolescents and adults with major depressive disorder (MDD) and evaluated the contribution of psychosocial factors to these differences. Adolescents and adults receiving treatment in the Department of Psychiatry were consecutively recruited between June 2023 and December 2024, including 115 adolescents (64.61%) and 63 adults (35.39%) in the final week-8 analysis set. Depressive symptom severity was assessed using the 24-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAMD-24).

item.title: From childhood to adulthood: an attempt to model long-term outcomes of ADHD using machine learning.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Childhood-onset attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) persists in 28% to 58% of individuals, and is associated with adverse long-term outcomes, like additional psychiatric diagnoses and lower educational attainment. Knowing early life predictors for adverse long-term outcomes might help develop preventive measures, but too few have been identified using conventional statistical models. The current study investigated the potential of machine learning in identifying predictors for ADHD persistence and long-term functioning of adults with childhood-onset ADHD.

item.title: Brain-computer interfaces in pediatric populations: research advances, application challenges, and future directions.
item.description: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) establish direct communication pathways between the brain and external devices. Leveraging the unique neuroplasticity of the developing brain, BCIs have emerged as a novel rehabilitative technology for children with neurodevelopmental disorders, including cerebral palsy, autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and perinatal brain injury.

item.title: Effects of diagnostic thresholds for gestational diabetes on perinatal mental health: Data from the GEMS randomised clinical trial.
item.description: AIM: To assess the effect of diagnosis using the lower International Association of the Diabetes and Pregnancy Study Groups (IADPSG) criteria compared with the higher New Zealand criteria on perinatal mental health. METHODS: Secondary analysis of the GEMS Trial, a randomised trial assessing optimum glycaemic diagnostic thresholds for gestational diabetes.

item.title: Genetic evidence for the psychosis continuum: polygenic score analysis.
item.description: BACKGROUND: The psychosis continuum conceptualises psychotic phenomena as existing on a spectrum from subclinical experiences to psychotic disorders. Despite epidemiological and clinical evidence in support of this model, few studies have examined polygenic liability across the severity continuum: from subclinical experiences to first-episode psychosis (FEP). AIMS: To map polygenic liability for schizophrenia (SCZ), bipolar disorder and major depressive disorder (MDD) across the psychosis continuum.

item.title: Genetic architecture of the personality meta-traits - stability and plasticity - and their transdiagnostic overlap with psychopathology.
item.description: BACKGROUND: The Five Factor Model (FFM) personality meta-traits, stability and plasticity, are thought to capture broad individual differences in the parameters of goal-directed, cybernetic mechanisms in the brain, which have implications for transdiagnostic psychopathology risk. It remains unknown whether these meta-traits represent genetically coherent dimensions. Here we conduct a genomic investigation into the FFM meta-traits and characterize their association with 11 psychiatric conditions.

item.title: Anterograde and retrograde amnesia following electroconvulsive therapy: A controlled longitudinal study accounting for time and depression.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) may be accompanied by amnesia. However, the extent to which different memory subtypes are affected is unclear, as well-controlled longitudinal studies are sparse. We aimed to investigate short- and long-term effects of ECT on different aspects of memory. METHODS: We recruited patients with depression referred to ECT (n = 31) or other treatment (n = 21) and healthy participants (n = 29).

item.title: Evaluating the Effect of Positive Childhood Experiences on the Risk of Psychiatric Disorders in Early Adulthood.
item.description: OBJECTIVE: While the negative impacts of traumatic childhood experiences are well established, less is known about whether positive childhood experiences (PCEs) contribute to long-term mental health. The aim of this study was to estimate the effect of PCEs on the risk of psychiatric disorders in early adulthood. METHODS: Participants included 3,499 children from the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children. Eligible participants were nonrandomly exposed to PCEs (e.g., "school enjoyment" or "feeling safe in neighborhood") between ages 0 and 17, measured as a score ranging from 0 to 10.

item.title: Single-cell, spatial, and machine learning analyses identify ANKIB1 as an oligodendrocyte-anchored palmitoylation-associated candidate biomarker of Alzheimer's disease.
item.description: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is characterized by progressive neurodegeneration and cognitive decline, yet most candidate therapies targeting amyloid-β have failed to robustly modify disease progression, underscoring an incomplete mechanistic understanding. Oligodendrocytes (ODCs) have recently emerged as active contributors to AD pathology, but the cell-type-specific role of protein S-palmitoylation - a reversible lipid post-translational modification regulating membrane targeting and trafficking - in AD remains uncharacterized.

item.title: [Alcoholic Liver Disease Hospital Admissions in Portugal: Demographic, Geographic and Temporal Patterns (2013 - 2023)].
item.description: INTRODUCTION: Excessive alcohol consumption is a major global public health concern, contributing to injuries, morbidity, disability, and premature mortality. Alcoholic liver disease (ALD), encompassing conditions from steatosis to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma, represents a substantial proportion of alcohol-related hospital admissions in Portugal. The aim of this study was to describe the temporal, demographic, and geographic patterns of ALD hospital admission episodes in Mainland Portugal between 2013 and 2023.

item.title: An innovative hybrid cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia approach to insomnia treatment: a retrospective chart review study.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Insomnia is a common and significant concern within family medicine; however, there is limited access to qualified sleep specialists trained in the first-line treatment: cognitive behavioral treatment for insomnia (CBT-I). Technology advancements allowed for "app delivery" of CBT-I, but platforms do not customize treatment. To our knowledge, DrLullaby was the first to offer a hybrid approach, to improve behavioral sleep medicine access, through "tech-enabled services," including telehealth sessions alongside our sleep data portal.

item.title: Feeling safe: an empirical-ethical analysis of vulnerability in (es)ketamine treatment.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Treatments with acute consciousness-altering effects, such as (es)ketamine, place patients in a state of heightened vulnerability with reduced capacity for self-advocacy and self-regulation. Since feeling safe is a precondition for consenting to begin, and remaining in, treatment, this raises distinct ethical demands on care. Which features of the setting enable patients to feel safe, and how patients' and clinicians' understandings of the treatment relate to these requirements, remains unclear.

item.title: Longitudinal changes in PCOS-related reproductive and metabolic markers in female patients with bipolar disorder: a six-month observational study.
item.description: OBJECTIVES: Female patients with bipolar disorder (BD) have a relatively high burden of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)-related reproductive abnormalities. This six-month longitudinal observational study aimed to examine changes in PCOS incidence and PCOS-related reproductive and metabolic markers in drug-naive female patients with BD managed without medication, with valproate (VPA), or with non-VPA mood stabilizers. METHODS: A total of 72 drug-naive female outpatients with BD were recruited, and 50 patients ultimately completed the six-month follow-up.

item.title: Poor mental health days and depressive disorders comparing non-caregivers, informal non-cancer caregivers, and informal caregivers of cancer patients: BRFSS 2022-23.
item.description: PURPOSE: Informal caregivers are increasing in number, especially those caring for cancer patients, and caregiving can affect both patient outcomes and caregiver well-being. This study sought to elucidate whether the mental health outcomes differed among informal cancer caregivers, informal non-cancer caregivers, and non-caregivers. METHODS: Data from 2022 and 2023 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance Surveys (BRFSS) were analyzed for 24 states administering the caregiving module.

item.title: Preoperative Sedation via Cecostomy Tube in an Autistic Adolescent: A Case Report.
item.description: Preoperative sedation of autistic children is frequently complicated by challenges in communication, sensory processing, and participation in medical care. We report a 40-kg, 13-year-old autistic boy with a preexisting cecostomy tube for chronic constipation, in whom previous oral and intramuscular sedation had failed due to agitation and physical aggression. Midazolam 10 mg (0.25 mg/kg) and ketamine 200 mg (5 mg/kg) were administered via cecostomy tube, producing sedation within 20 minutes. Dental rehabilitation under general anesthesia proceeded uneventfully.

item.title: Body dysmorphic disorder in autistic youth: clinical characteristics, treatment outcomes, and clinical adaptations.
item.description: Body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) is a prevalent and often disabling condition with onset typically occurring during adolescence. To date, little is known about the presentation or treatment of BDD in autistic youth. Using data from two specialist clinics, the current study compared the clinical characteristics and treatment outcomes of autistic (n = 62) and non-autistic (n = 240) youth with BDD. The groups showed broadly similar clinical presentations, with several notable differences.

item.title: Disparities in Social Determinants of Health and Health Outcomes Among Autistic Individuals Without Intellectual Disability in Middle-to-Late Adulthood.
item.description: Autism is increasingly recognized across the lifespan, yet little is known about how structural social disadvantage contributes to long-term health risks among autistic adults in middle and later adulthood. Participants were identified from the UK Biobank study, comprising 576 autistic adults with no intellectual disability and an average of 15.2 years of education, and 5,760 controls matched on age, sex, residing area, race, and educational attainment.

item.title: Risk and protective factors of solitary cannabis use among Canadian secondary school students: findings from the COMPASS study.
item.description: INTRODUCTION: Solitary cannabis use has become increasingly prevalent among youth in Canada and is linked to both mental and behavioural concerns. This study seeks to fill current gaps in the literature by examining the factors associated with solitary cannabis use to understand the complexities of specific contexts in which use occurs and improve prevention efforts targeted towards behaviours that are associated with greater health impacts and riskier behaviours.

item.title: Suicide in People With Co-occurring Substance Use and Mental Health Conditions: An Integrative Literature Review to Inform Risk Formulation in Mental Health Nursing.
item.description: People with co-occurring substance use and mental health conditions experience disproportionately high levels of suicidal ideation, attempts and deaths compared with those with either condition alone, yet guidance for suicide risk formulation in this group is limited. This integrative literature review synthesised evidence on suicidality in adults with co-occurring conditions, identified risk and protective factors, and refined risk formulation approaches for mental health nursing.

item.title: Implementation evaluation of a Massachusetts pilot program designed to reduce overdose deaths among Black and Latino men returning from incarceration.
item.description: INTRODUCTION AND CONTEXT: In response to rising and disproportionate overdose deaths, a Massachusetts agency developed a program model (CARE) that incorporated evidence-based and evidence-informed practices to support recovery and overdose prevention for Black and Latino men returning to their communities from incarceration. Recruitment of Black and Latino men at risk of overdose was intended to begin in local jails prior to release.

item.title: Impact of opioid agonist therapies on non-fatal and fatal overdose: treatment patterns among individuals with opioid use disorder in Ontario, Canada.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Although opioid agonist therapies (OAT) including buprenorphine extended-release (BUP-XR), transmucosal buprenorphine (TM-BUP), methadone and slow-release oral morphine (SROM) are effective and established medications for opioid use disorder (MOUD) available in Canada, differences in opioid-related overdose (OD) risk reduction across OAT types and patterns of treatment use are not well characterized. OBJECTIVE: To assess the impact of OAT on opioid-related non-fatal and fatal OD among individuals with OUD in Ontario, Canada, and to examine patterns of OAT use.

item.title: Impact of an addiction medicine consult service on medications for opioid use disorder initiation in hospitalized patients.
item.description: OBJECTIVE: The number of overdose deaths rose by 60 percent between 2019 and 2021. Medications for opioid use disorder (MOUD) have been associated with reduced overdoses and opioid-related hospitalizations. Hospital addiction medicine consult services (AMCSs) have been shown to reduce all-cause 90-day mortality post-discharge. This study aimed to expand on the impact of AMCS on the initiation of MOUD in inpatients. Design, setting, patients/participants, interventions, main outcome measure: This study is a retrospective, single site, multicenter, cohort study conducted at two sites.

item.title: OUR crisis: Evolution of a third-year medical student opioid epidemic-themed inter-clerkship week to reflect the landscape of pain and addiction care.
item.description: OBJECTIVE: A week-long themed interclerkship curricular experience was designed to reframe THE Opioid Epidemic as "OUR Opioid Epidemic," humanize and normalize opioid use disorder and pain, and motivate a shift in attitudes, knowledge, comfort, and perceived skills. DESIGN: This was a prospective cohort study with pre- and post-curriculum surveys. SETTING: The curriculum was delivered at a medical school associated with a large health system over 6 academic years.

item.title: Digital twins for personalized management of opioid use disorder: A future outlook.
item.description: INTRODUCTION: The opioid crisis, affecting over 16 million individuals globally and causing approximately 450,000 deaths annually, underscores the urgent need for personalized treatment approaches for opioid use disorder (OUD). Current treatments, such as medication-assisted therapy, suffer from low retention rates and variable responses due to individual differences. METHODS: This study proposes a digital twin framework, integrating genetic profiles, eg, OPRM1 variants, electronic health records, ecological momentary assessments, and real-time physiological data from wearables.

item.title: Impact of Methamphetamine Use on Injury Characteristics and Postoperative Outcomes in Upper Extremity Fractures.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Methamphetamine use in orthopedic trauma carries an indeterminate risk, with prior studies suggesting increased rates of deep vein thrombosis and elevated mortality. Upper extremity fractures (UEFs) have distinct mechanisms of injury and operative risk. This study evaluates outcomes following operative management of UEFs in patients with and without documented methamphetamine use.

item.title: Key Decision Points for Personalization and Customization in Self-Guided Digital Suicide Prevention: Qualitative Interview Study.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Young adults in the United States experience high rates of suicidal thoughts and behaviors (STB) but low engagement with traditional care, highlighting the need for accessible and scalable digital interventions. Self-guided digital safety planning interventions (SPIs) can expand access to support but introduce important decisions about what content to deliver, when systems should intervene, and how users retain control over system actions.

item.title: "Am I a candidate for magic mushrooms?" A mystery shopper study of Oregon psilocybin service centers.
item.description: INTRODUCTION: Oregon is the first US state to permit supervised psilocybin services through a nonmedical, wellness-based model. We examined what prospective clients with psychiatric histories encounter when contacting service centers, including how staff communicate about safety, eligibility, and cost. METHODS: We conducted a mystery shopper study of 26 licensed service centers in Oregon (7/2025-9/2025), 4 of which closed before calls began, leaving 22 in the sample. We reviewed websites and conducted 2 waves of scripted phone calls portraying adults with depression.

item.title: Living with and caring for somatic symptom disorders: a qualitative interview-study with patients and GPs using a deductive-inductive content analytic approach.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Persistent physical symptoms are common in general practice and often occur as part of a somatic symptom disorder. Patients suffering from somatic symptom disorders and their general practitioners (GPs) often experience barriers to mutual trust and effective care. Frequently, studies using a one-sided perspective bear mutual accusation about shortcomings of the respective other side.

item.title: Low-dose colchicine: a potential augmenting agent in the treatment of refractory mood disorders.
item.description: Treatment-resistant mood disorders, including major depressive disorder (MDD) and bipolar disorder (BD), remain a significant clinical challenge. A confluence of emerging evidence implicates chronic low-grade inflammation in the pathophysiology of at least a subset of mood disorders, potentially mediating their poor response to traditional therapies. Colchicine, a well-established anti-inflammatory agent used in gout and more recently (at low dose) cardiovascular disease, inhibits microtubule polymerisation and suppresses NLRP3 inflammasome activation.

item.title: Adult Attention Deficit-Hyperactivity Disorder.
item.description: Attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a medical condition that is present in approximately 2.5% of adults worldwide and manifests in a variety of different ways across the lifespan. Adults with ADHD often have coexisting psychiatric disorders such as anxiety, mood, sleep, substance use, and personality disorders and are at increased risk for coexisting somatic conditions such as obesity, cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease, type 1 and type 2 diabetes, and immune and inflammatory conditions.

item.title: The Evolving Paradigm of Autism: Folate Receptor Autoimmunity deranging Epigenetic Programming in fetal and postnatal Brain Development.
item.description: This review on autism provides a summary of the multiple genetic, epigenetic and environmental changes setting the stage for disturbed brain development due to aberrant synaptogenesis and corticogenesis during the prenatal and post-natal periods. The emphasis is placed on nonmendelian transmission driven by epigenetics. Folate deficiency appears to play a critical role in influencing many of the structural changes contributing to developmental deficits.

item.title: To Collapse or not to Collapse Multiple Measures of the Same Psychological Construct: A Demonstration Across 14 Independent Studies of Autistic and Non-Autistic Children.
item.description: Large data repositories provide a valuable opportunity to combine multiple independent studies, creating large samples that can address questions not achievable within a single study. However, independent studies often use different instruments to measure the same behavior or psychological construct, such as cognitive ability, social functioning, or psychopathology. Investigators often combine samples that include different instruments under the assumption that instruments assessing the same construct capture the same underlying phenomenon.
